title: Coordinates
part: I: Geometry and mechanics in flat spacetime
one_line_summary: Argues that physics should ideally be coordinate-free, then concedes that coordinates are needed and uses plane polar coordinates to show how components and basis vectors transform, why the natural coordinate basis vector e_theta grows with r, how coordinate (holonomic) and normalized non-coordinate bases differ via loop closure and the Lie bracket, why the position vector must be retired, and how non-Euclidean spaces (Minkowski, the sphere) break Euclid's circle and triangle results.
role_in_book: Third chapter of Part I, sitting between Chapter 2 (vectors, components and Lorentz transformation laws in flat spacetime) and Chapters 4-5 (one-forms, tensors and the metric). It generalizes the Chapter 2 transformation rules from Lorentz boosts to arbitrary, nonlinear coordinate changes, which is the step that makes the machinery usable in curved spacetime. It plants several seeds that the book harvests later: basis vectors as derivative operators (Chapter 31), non-coordinate orthonormal frames (Chapter 10), velocity as a tangent to a world line (Chapter 7), derivatives of basis vectors that become connection coefficients (Chapters 7 and 9), and intrinsic curvature tests with circles and triangles (Chapters 11 and 30). It is short and light on formalism by design: a vocabulary chapter rather than a derivation chapter.

assumed_background.topic: Vectors written as components times basis vectors, X = X^mu e_mu, with the Einstein summation convention
Transformation laws for vector components (eqn 2.11) and for basis vectors (eqn 2.25) under Lorentz transformations
Minkowski line element, proper time, and the relativistic form of Newton's second law f = dp/dtau
Partial derivatives holding variables fixed, and the multivariable chain rule
Matrix multiplication, matrix inverses, Jacobian matrices
Plane polar coordinates and basic trigonometric identities
Dot product, length and angle between vectors in ordinary space
Rotating reference frames and the centrifugal and Coriolis pseudo-forces
Great circles, sphere surface area 4 pi R^2, radian measure of angles
Euclidean plane geometry results: circle circumference 2 pi r and triangle angle sum pi

learning_objectives: Reader can explain why coordinate-free (geometric) statements of physical laws are preferred, using the example of Newton's second law acquiring centrifugal and Coriolis terms in a rotating frame.
Reader can define Euclidean space through the metric components delta_mu_nu and use it to compute lengths and angles.
Reader can build the Jacobian matrices between Cartesian and plane polar coordinates and use them to transform the components of an infinitesimal displacement.
Reader can derive the coordinate basis vectors e_r and e_theta from the basis-vector transformation law and show that e_theta has length r.
Reader can distinguish a coordinate (holonomic) basis from a non-coordinate (anholonomic) basis, both by the closed-loop walking picture and by computing the Lie bracket.
Reader can identify coordinate basis vectors with partial-derivative operators via the chain rule along a parametrized path, and compute [e_hat_r, e_hat_theta] = -e_hat_theta / r.
Reader can explain why the position vector x = x^mu e_mu is not a vector under general coordinate changes while infinitesimal displacements are, and state the slogan that coordinates are not vectors.
Reader can state what makes a space non-Euclidean, recognise Minkowski spacetime as non-Euclidean yet flat, and write its line element in (-,+,+,+) form.
Reader can quote and use the sphere results C = 2 pi r sinc(r/R) and angle sum = pi + A/R^2, and recover Euclid's results in the small-circle or small-triangle limit.
Reader can extract a curvature K = 1/R^2 from the deficit of circle circumferences in the limit of small circles, and prove Girard's theorem by counting lune areas.
Reader can transform the Minkowski line element into a uniformly rotating frame and interpret the new metric components.

teaching_approach.summary: A brisk, conversational vocabulary chapter. It opens by questioning whether coordinates are needed at all, grants that practical problems force them on us, and then works almost entirely inside one familiar example, plane polar coordinates, so that every new idea (transformation matrices, coordinate basis, non-coordinate basis, Lie bracket, vectors as derivatives) is met on known ground. Surprising outputs are embraced rather than hidden: the unnormalized e_theta is presented as a feature, and a loop-walking picture explains why. The chapter then clears away the position vector with a geographic counterexample and closes with non-Euclidean geometry stated (not proved) in example boxes, handing the proofs and a first curvature definition to guided exercises. Humor (Shakespeare, the Death Star) and margin slogans carry the informal voice.
narrative_arc: Provocation: ask whether coordinates are even needed; a law like f = dp/dtau is frame-independent, while a rotating frame dresses it with pseudo-forces.

Concession: symmetries and frame-specific values drag us back to coordinates, so the authors list the vocabulary still to be defined: Euclidean and non-Euclidean space, Cartesian coordinates, and coordinate versus non-coordinate bases.
Model: Euclidean space defined by the identity metric delta_mu_nu, giving the usual scalar product, length and angle; restrict to the plane.
Two descriptions of the same plane: Cartesian (x, y) and polar (r, theta), with the familiar conversion formulas (Fig. 3.1).
Formalism reused: the Chapter 2 component law, now with a coordinate-dependent Jacobian, applied to displacement components (Example 3.1).
Formalism reused again: the basis-vector law gives e_r and e_theta (Example 3.2), which turn out not to be unit vectors (e_theta . e_theta = r^2).
Reinterpretation: the growth of e_theta is required for a coordinate (holonomic) basis; normalized vectors form a non-coordinate basis; a closed-loop walk distinguishes them (Figs. 3.2, 3.3).
Check via a new representation: tangent vectors as derivative operators along a path, e_mu = partial/partial x^mu, making the Lie bracket computable (Example 3.3).

Clearing debris: the position vector fails the general transformation law because nonlinear coordinate changes have coordinate-dependent coefficients; a New York to Tokyo arrow would leave the Earth's surface; keep coordinates as labels and infinitesimal displacements as vectors.
Application to geometry: non-Euclidean spaces, first Minkowski spacetime (non-Euclidean but flat), then the sphere where circle circumference and triangle angle sums deviate (Example 3.4).

Consolidation through exercises: inverse basis transformation, derivatives of polar basis vectors, curvature from shrinking circles, Girard's theorem by lune areas, and the Minkowski metric in a rotating frame.
signature_moves: Open a technical chapter by doubting that its subject is needed, then justify it pragmatically.
Apply a known formula mechanically, let it produce an unexpected result (a basis vector whose length is r), and reframe the surprise as a necessary property.
Explain holonomic versus anholonomic bases by walking a four-step loop on a polar grid and checking whether it closes.
Pattern-match the chain rule d/dlambda = (dx^mu/dlambda) partial_mu against X = X^mu e_mu to identify basis vectors with derivative operators, which turns the Lie bracket into a one-line calculation.
Use everyday geography (an arrow from New York to Tokyo tunnelling through the Earth) to show that finite displacements do not live in a curved space.
Condense a caution into a margin slogan: coordinates are not vectors.
State striking non-Euclidean results in an example box and defer their proofs to scaffolded exercises that also introduce a limit definition of curvature.
Lighten dense material with literary and pop-culture jokes and with a fair-credit historical footnote.

sections.title: Chapter opening: do we need coordinates?
sections.summary: After a Shakespeare epigraph about girdling the Earth, the authors contrast a coordinate-free vector law (f = dp/dtau) with its component version in a rotating frame, which acquires centrifugal and Coriolis terms although the physics is unchanged. They advocate geometric statements whenever possible but admit that particular problems, frame-specific values and symmetries require coordinates, and list the terms the chapter will define.
key_moves: A vector equation relates arrows in spacetime and holds in any coordinates.
Rewriting it in a rotating frame produces pseudo-force terms: coordinate artefacts, not new physics.
Coordinates remain necessary for frame-specific values and for exploiting symmetry.

sections.title: Coordinates in Euclidean space
sections.summary: Defines Euclidean space as the space whose scalar product uses the identity metric delta_mu_nu, so lengths and angles take their school forms, and specializes to the plane. The plane is labelled either by Cartesian (x, y) or plane polar (r, theta) coordinates. The Chapter 2 transformation law for components, now written with a Jacobian of partial derivatives, converts displacement components dx, dy into dr, dtheta (Example 3.1), and the opposite law for basis vectors produces e_r and e_theta in terms of e_x and e_y (Example 3.2). These differ from the textbook unit vectors: e_theta has squared length r^2.
concepts: Jacobian matrix of a coordinate transformation
key_moves: Scalar product X . Y = delta_mu_nu X^mu Y^nu defines length and angle.
Reuse the Chapter 2 law with Lambda^{mu'}_nu = partial x^{mu'} / partial x^nu, which is now position dependent.
Compute both Jacobians (derivatives of x, y with respect to r, theta, and the reverse) and assemble the displacement transformation matrix.
Transform basis vectors with the inverse-direction Jacobian to get e_r = cos theta e_x + sin theta e_y and e_theta = -r sin theta e_x + r cos theta e_y.
Compare with the normalized textbook vectors and compute e_r . e_r = 1, e_theta . e_theta = r^2.

sections.title: Coordinate versus non-coordinate bases and vectors as derivatives (end of 3.1)
sections.summary: Explains why the growing e_theta is desirable. The unhatted vectors are a coordinate (holonomic) basis; the normalized ones are a non-coordinate (anholonomic) basis. The loose test is to walk a closed loop of steps along the basis directions: with coordinate basis vectors the loop closes because the outer arc is automatically longer, while with normalized vectors equal arcs at different radii subtend different angles and the loop fails to close (Figs. 3.2, 3.3). Example 3.3 makes this precise by writing the derivative of a function along a path as a sum of components times partial derivatives, identifying e_mu with partial/partial x^mu, and computing that partial derivatives commute whereas the normalized pair has bracket -e_hat_theta/r. Detailed treatment is deferred to Chapters 10 and 31.
concepts: loop-closure test for a coordinate basis
key_moves: Norm growth of e_theta is a feature: steps along e_theta must cover more distance at larger r.
Closed loop +e_r, +e_theta, -e_r, -e_theta returns to its start for coordinate basis vectors, not for normalized ones.
Chain rule along x^mu(lambda): df/dlambda = (dx^mu/dlambda) partial f / partial x^mu, valid for any f, so the operator itself has the shape of a vector.
Identify e_mu with partial_mu; coordinate basis vectors commute by equality of mixed partial derivatives.
Apply the commutator of e_hat_r = partial_r and e_hat_theta = (1/r) partial_theta to a test function to get -e_hat_theta / r.

sections.title: Farewell to the position vector
sections.summary: The position vector worked in special relativity because Lorentz transformations are linear, but in general relativity it is abandoned. If coordinates are related by x' = A x with coefficients that depend on position, the Jacobian is not A and the coordinates do not obey the vector transformation law; only linear homogeneous maps (Lorentz boosts, rotations) are safe. Geometrically, on a curved surface a finite displacement is not even in the space: the straight arrow from New York to Tokyo runs through the Earth, whereas a path of infinitesimal steps stays on the surface. Coordinates stay as event labels, infinitesimal displacements stay as vectors, and velocity will be rebuilt as a tangent to a world line in Chapter 7.
concepts: four-velocity as tangent to a world line
key_moves: State the general vector law X^{mu'} = (partial x^{mu'} / partial x^nu) X^nu.
Coordinates themselves transform through coefficients that depend on position, so partial x^{mu'} / partial x^nu differs from those coefficients and x^mu is not a vector.
Special case: constant coefficients (Lorentz, rotations) rescue the position vector.
Geographic picture: a finite chord leaves the surface; a chain of infinitesimal displacements does not.
Reassure: velocity survives as the tangent to a world line; infinitesimal displacement still transforms correctly.

sections.title: Non-Euclidean space
sections.summary: Defines non-Euclidean space negatively, as any space whose metric is not delta_mu_nu, and offers Minkowski spacetime with ds^2 = -dt^2 + dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2 as the first example, a (3+1)-dimensional space. Example 3.4 then shows Euclid's results failing on the surface of a sphere of radius R: a circle of surface radius r has circumference 2 pi r sinc(r/R), and by Girard's theorem the angles of a spherical triangle of area A sum to pi + A/R^2. Both reduce to the Euclidean values for small r or small A; proofs are assigned as Exercises 3.3 and 3.4.
concepts: circumference of a circle on a sphere
key_moves: Non-Euclidean is defined by the metric, not by curvature, so flat Minkowski spacetime qualifies.
On a sphere a circle's circumference falls short of 2 pi r, by an amount controlled by r/R.
Triangle angle sums exceed pi by the triangle's area divided by R^2.
Euclid is recovered as a small-size limit, hinting that curvature is visible only on scales comparable to R.

sections.title: Chapter summary and exercises
sections.summary: The summary restates that Euclidean space may be described in several coordinate systems, that coordinate basis vectors obtained by transformation have vanishing Lie brackets unlike a non-coordinate basis, and that a non-Euclidean metric such as Minkowski's may still be flat. Five exercises follow: inverting the polar basis transformation, differentiating polar basis vectors, extracting curvature from small circles, proving Girard's theorem with lunes (Fig. 3.6), and writing the Minkowski metric in a rotating frame.
key_moves: Curvature K = 1/R^2 is defined operationally as the small-circle limit of the circumference deficit.
Girard's theorem follows from area bookkeeping: six lune-minus-triangle strips plus two triangles tile the sphere.
A rotating frame gives a non-diagonal, position-dependent Minkowski metric, closing the loop with the chapter opening.

concepts.name: coordinate-free formulation of physical laws
concepts.definition: Writing physical laws as relations between geometric objects (vectors, tensors) that do not refer to any coordinate system, so the statement holds unchanged in every frame; components appear only when a basis is chosen.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by Newton's second law f = dp/dtau, which is a relation between two spacetime arrows; in a rotating frame its components pick up centrifugal and Coriolis terms although nothing physical has changed.
concepts.notes: The ideal the whole book pursues; Part V returns to it with forms and index-free geometry.

concepts.name: rotating reference frame
concepts.definition: A frame whose spatial axes turn at angular speed Omega relative to an inertial frame; in it, laws written in components acquire pseudo-force terms, and the Minkowski metric picks up cross terms coupling dt' to dx' and dy' plus a g_tt that depends on distance from the rotation axis (none of the components depend on t').
concepts.how_introduced: Used at the opening as the example of coordinates complicating a simple law, and returned to in Exercise 3.5, where the coordinate change to a rotating frame is applied to the Minkowski line element.
formulas: x = x'\cos\Omega t' - y'\sin\Omega t',\; y = x'\sin\Omega t' + y'\cos\Omega t'

concepts.name: Euclidean space
concepts.definition: An n-dimensional space of points in which the scalar product of two vectors is the plain sum of products of their components in Cartesian coordinates, i.e. the metric components are delta_mu_nu; lengths, angles and Euclid's theorems (angle sum pi, circumference 2 pi r) follow.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined at the start of Section 3.1 via its scalar product, with length and angle derived from it, and tied to Euclid's Elements; the authors immediately specialise to the plane.

concepts.name: Euclidean metric
concepts.definition: The metric whose components in Cartesian coordinates form the identity matrix, delta_mu_nu, so X . Y = delta_mu_nu X^mu Y^nu and ds^2 = delta_mu_nu dx^mu dx^nu.
concepts.how_introduced: Given in a margin note as the identity-matrix form of the metric in the scalar product, then used in Section 3.3 as the benchmark against which non-Euclidean spaces are defined.
concepts.notes: The components are delta_mu_nu only in Cartesian coordinates; in polar coordinates the same flat metric has components diag(1, r^2), a point the chapter implies through eqn 3.11 but does not state.

concepts.name: Cartesian coordinates
concepts.definition: Coordinates that label each point of Euclidean space by its signed distances along mutually perpendicular straight axes, so that the metric components are the identity.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced historically (Descartes, 1637) with Fig. 3.1(a), a grid with a point located by (x0, y0).

concepts.name: plane polar coordinates
aliases: cylindrical polar coordinates (book's slip in Example 3.1)
concepts.definition: Coordinates (r, theta) on the Euclidean plane giving the distance from the origin and the angle from a reference axis, related to Cartesian ones by x = r cos theta, y = r sin theta.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the alternative description of the same plane in Fig. 3.1(b); then used as the single running example for every idea in Section 3.1.
formulas: x = r\cos\theta,\; y = r\sin\theta,\; r = (x^2+y^2)^{1/2},\; \tan\theta = y/x

concepts.name: curvilinear coordinates
concepts.definition: Coordinates whose coordinate lines are not all straight and mutually orthogonal with uniform spacing, so the line element is not simply the sum of squared coordinate differentials (for polar coordinates ds^2 = dr^2 + r^2 dtheta^2, not dr^2 + dtheta^2).
concepts.how_introduced: Named in a margin note that calls polar coordinates the first example and points out that Pythagoras fails in its naive form.

concepts.name: Jacobian matrix of a coordinate transformation
concepts.definition: The matrix of partial derivatives partial x^{mu'} / partial x^nu between two coordinate systems; it maps components of vectors at a point, depends on position for nonlinear transformations, and its inverse is partial x^nu / partial x^{mu'}.
concepts.how_introduced: Carried over from the Lorentz matrix of Chapter 2 and computed explicitly for Cartesian to polar coordinates in Example 3.1, where its entries depend on r and theta.
concepts.notes: The chapter never shows explicitly that the matrices built from eqns 3.4 and 3.5 are inverses; multiplying them is a worthwhile check.

concepts.name: transformation law for vector components
concepts.definition: Under a change of coordinates the components of a vector at a point change by the Jacobian: X^{mu'} = (partial x^{mu'} / partial x^nu) X^nu. Any set of quantities that obeys this is a vector.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 2 (eqn 2.11), rewritten with partial derivatives in eqn 3.3, used on displacement components in Example 3.1 and elevated in Section 3.2 to the test that the position vector fails.
prerequisites: Jacobian matrix of a coordinate transformation

concepts.name: transformation law for basis vectors
concepts.definition: Basis vectors transform with the inverse Jacobian, e_{mu'} = (partial x^nu / partial x^{mu'}) e_nu, so that the vector X = X^mu e_mu itself is unchanged by the coordinate change.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from eqn 2.25 as the opposite of the component law (eqn 3.7) and used in Example 3.2 to generate the polar basis vectors.

concepts.name: infinitesimal displacement vector
aliases: displacement vector d x = dx^mu e_mu
concepts.definition: The vector dx = dx^mu e_mu joining a point to an infinitesimally nearby point; its components transform with the Jacobian and it lies in the space even when the space is curved.
concepts.how_introduced: Used as the test case for the component transformation in Example 3.1, and in Section 3.2 as the well-behaved replacement for the finite position vector.

concepts.name: coordinate basis
concepts.definition: A basis of vector fields obtained from a coordinate system, e_mu = partial/partial x^mu, each vector pointing along a coordinate line and sized so that one unit of it advances that coordinate by one; its members have vanishing Lie brackets.
concepts.how_introduced: Arrived at by plugging polar coordinates into the basis-vector law, noticing e_theta has length r, and explaining this with a closed loop that only closes if the theta-step grows with r; then confirmed by writing e_mu as partial derivatives.

concepts.name: non-coordinate basis
concepts.definition: A basis of vector fields that cannot be written as partial derivatives with respect to any coordinates; at least one Lie bracket among its members is non-zero, so stepping around a small loop along its vectors fails to close.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced by contrast with the unhatted polar vectors: the normalized textbook pair e_hat_r, e_hat_theta is shown to have a non-zero bracket and a non-closing loop.
concepts.notes: Returns in Chapter 10 as orthonormal measurement frames (vielbeins).

concepts.name: orthonormal polar basis
concepts.definition: The unit vectors e_hat_r = cos theta e_x + sin theta e_y and e_hat_theta = -sin theta e_x + cos theta e_y, orthogonal and of unit length at every point; as derivative operators e_hat_r = partial_r and e_hat_theta = (1/r) partial_theta.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted as what elementary treatments use, then shown to be a non-coordinate basis.

concepts.name: metric components as basis-vector dot products
concepts.definition: The metric components in a basis are the scalar products of the basis vectors; for the polar coordinate basis g_rr = 1, g_theta_theta = r^2, g_r_theta = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Implicit in eqn 3.11, where the norms of e_r and e_theta are computed; the general statement is made in Chapter 5.

concepts.name: Lie bracket
concepts.definition: For vector fields viewed as derivative operators, [X, Y] f = X(Y f) - Y(X f); the result is again a vector field, and for small steps it measures by how much a loop of flows along X, Y, -X, -Y fails to close.
concepts.how_introduced: Named loosely during the loop discussion, then computed properly in Example 3.3 once basis vectors are partial derivatives; the non-zero bracket of the normalized polar vectors is derived on a test function.
concepts.notes: Formalized in Part V with Lie derivatives (Chapter 33).

concepts.name: loop-closure test for a coordinate basis
concepts.definition: Step along basis vector field A, then B, then back along A, then back along B; the loop closes (to second order in step size) for every pair exactly when the basis vector fields commute, i.e. when they form a coordinate basis.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered as the intuitive meaning of holonomic, illustrated on a quarter-disk polar grid in Fig. 3.3 with loops ABCDE.

concepts.name: parametrized curve
concepts.definition: A map from a parameter lambda (here in [0, 1]) to points x^mu(lambda) of the space, tracing a path.
concepts.how_introduced: Set up in Example 3.3 so that a function can be evaluated and differentiated along the path.

concepts.name: directional derivative along a curve
concepts.definition: The rate of change of a scalar function along a parametrized curve, obtained by the chain rule as the curve's tangent components times the partial derivatives of the function.
concepts.how_introduced: Computed in Example 3.3 for an arbitrary function f(x^mu) on a path x^mu(lambda); stripping off f gives an operator.

concepts.name: tangent vectors as derivative operators
concepts.definition: The modern definition of a tangent vector as a directional-derivative operator: the operator d/dlambda along a curve has components dx^mu/dlambda in the basis partial/partial x^mu, so basis vectors are identified with partial derivatives.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as a trick suggested by the resemblance between the chain-rule operator and X^mu e_mu; its full justification is postponed to Chapter 31.

concepts.name: position vector
concepts.definition: The object x = x^mu e_mu built from the coordinates of a point; it behaves as a vector only under linear homogeneous coordinate changes and is not a legitimate vector in general curved-space or curvilinear settings.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from its successful use under Lorentz transformations in Chapter 2, then retired in Section 3.2 by showing that nonlinear coordinate changes spoil its transformation and by the New York to Tokyo picture.

concepts.name: coordinates are not vectors
concepts.definition: Coordinates are labels of points (events); the array x^mu does not transform by the Jacobian under general coordinate changes and so is not the component set of any vector, while infinitesimal coordinate differences dx^mu are.
concepts.how_introduced: Condensed into a margin slogan after the position-vector argument of Section 3.2; footnote 4 points back to Example 3.1 as a concrete failure.

concepts.name: linear homogeneous transformation
concepts.definition: A coordinate change x^{mu'} = A^{mu'}_nu x^nu with constant coefficients (no shift and no position dependence), such as Lorentz boosts and rotations; for these the Jacobian equals A and coordinates do transform like vector components.
concepts.how_introduced: Named as the special case in which the position vector survives, explaining why special relativity could use it.
prerequisites: Jacobian matrix of a coordinate transformation

concepts.name: tangent vector
concepts.definition: A vector attached to a single point of a space, representing an infinitesimal displacement or a rate of change along a curve through that point; on a curved space such vectors lie in the tangent space at the point rather than in the space itself.
concepts.how_introduced: Implicit in the New York to Tokyo argument: finite arrows leave the Earth's surface, while chains of infinitesimal displacements stay on it.
concepts.notes: The chapter does not use the words tangent space; Chapter 31 and Appendix C supply them.

concepts.name: four-velocity as tangent to a world line
concepts.definition: The velocity vector of a particle defined geometrically as the tangent vector to its world line parametrized by proper time, rather than as the derivative of a position vector.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered as reassurance that dropping the position vector does not destroy velocity; the construction is deferred to Chapter 7.

concepts.name: non-Euclidean space
concepts.definition: In this book's usage, any space whose metric is not the Euclidean delta_mu_nu (equivalently, whose line element cannot be brought to that form); this includes both indefinite flat metrics such as Minkowski's and curved spaces such as the sphere.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined negatively at the start of Section 3.3 and illustrated first by Minkowski spacetime, then by the surface of a sphere where Euclid's theorems fail.
concepts.notes: In mathematics 'non-Euclidean geometry' usually means curved (spherical or hyperbolic) geometry; the book widens the term to signature as well.

concepts.name: Minkowski spacetime
concepts.definition: The flat spacetime of special relativity with line element ds^2 = -dt^2 + dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2 in inertial coordinates (c = 1): three space dimensions and one time dimension with an indefinite metric eta_mu_nu.
concepts.how_introduced: Given as the first example of a non-Euclidean space and noted in the summary to be flat despite being non-Euclidean.

concepts.name: flat space
concepts.definition: A space (or spacetime) with zero intrinsic curvature, so that coordinates exist in which the metric components are constant everywhere; flatness is independent of the signature and of how complicated the metric looks in a particular coordinate system.
concepts.how_introduced: Asserted in the chapter summary (a non-Euclidean metric can still be flat, as Minkowski's is); no test for flatness is given until the Riemann tensor in Chapter 11.

concepts.name: great circle
concepts.definition: The intersection of a sphere with a plane through its centre; great circles are the geodesics (locally shortest paths) on the sphere.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to build the spherical triangle of Fig. 3.5 and the lune construction of Fig. 3.6.

concepts.name: spherical triangle
concepts.definition: A region on a sphere bounded by arcs of three great circles, with interior angles alpha_1, alpha_2, alpha_3 measured between the tangent directions of the arcs at each vertex.
concepts.how_introduced: Drawn in Fig. 3.5 as the small cap near the top where three great circles cross.

concepts.name: circumference of a circle on a sphere
concepts.definition: A circle whose radius r is measured along the surface of a sphere of radius R has circumference C = 2 pi R sin(r/R) = 2 pi r sinc(r/R), which is less than 2 pi r and tends to it as r/R goes to zero.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated in Example 3.4 with the Death Star cartoon of Fig. 3.4 as an everyday failure of a Euclidean formula; its proof by elementary geometry is Exercise 3.3.

concepts.name: Girard's theorem
concepts.definition: The interior angles of a spherical triangle of area A on a sphere of radius R sum to pi + A/R^2; the excess over pi is proportional to area, and vanishes for triangles small compared with R^2.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated in Example 3.4 with Fig. 3.5, credited in a footnote to Thomas Harriot, and proved in Exercise 3.4 by decomposing the sphere into lune strips (Fig. 3.6).

concepts.name: lune
concepts.definition: The region of a sphere between two great semicircles meeting at antipodal points with angle alpha; on a unit sphere its area is 2 alpha.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears in Exercise 3.4 as the strips (lune minus triangle, area 2 alpha_1 - A) that tile the sphere outside two antipodal triangles.
concepts.notes: The word lune is ours; the book calls them strips.

concepts.name: Gaussian curvature
concepts.definition: A number at each point of a surface measuring its intrinsic curvature; for a sphere of radius R it is K = 1/R^2, and it can be obtained from how much the circumference of small circles falls short of 2 pi r.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced only in Exercise 3.3, which rewrites the circle result using K = 1/R^2 and extracts K as a small-circle limit.
prerequisites: circumference of a circle on a sphere
concepts.notes: Developed properly in Chapter 11 (Riemann tensor) and Chapter 30 (classical curvature).

concepts.name: derivatives of basis vectors
concepts.definition: In curvilinear coordinates the basis vectors change from point to point; for plane polar coordinates the partial derivatives of e_r and e_theta are again combinations of e_r and e_theta with position-dependent coefficients.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 3.2 has the reader compute them, foreshadowing connection coefficients.
concepts.notes: The coefficients are the Christoffel symbols of flat polar coordinates (Gamma^theta_{r theta} = 1/r, Gamma^r_{theta theta} = -r), met in Chapters 7 and 9.

concepts.name: Einstein summation convention
concepts.definition: A repeated index appearing once up and once down in a term is summed over its range, so X^mu e_mu means the sum over mu.
concepts.how_introduced: Used without comment throughout; the margin note on the Euclidean metric invokes it explicitly.

key_equations.name: Newton's second law as a vector relation
key_equations.meaning: A relation between spacetime vectors valid in every frame; its component form becomes messier in a rotating frame although the physics is the same.
key_equations.symbols: f four-force; p four-momentum; tau proper time

key_equations.name: Euclidean scalar product
key_equations.meaning: Defines Euclidean space: the metric components in Cartesian coordinates are the identity.
key_equations.symbols: X, Y vectors; delta_mu_nu Euclidean metric components

key_equations.name: Length and angle from the scalar product
key_equations.meaning: The metric alone fixes lengths and angles.
key_equations.symbols: vartheta angle between X and Y

key_equations.name: Cartesian-polar relations
key_equations.latex: x = r\cos\theta,\quad y = r\sin\theta,\quad r = (x^2+y^2)^{1/2},\quad \tan\theta = y/x
key_equations.meaning: Connects the two labellings of the same point of the plane.
key_equations.symbols: r distance from origin; theta angle from the x axis

key_equations.name: Component transformation law
key_equations.meaning: Vector components at a point transform with the Jacobian of the coordinate change; this generalizes the Lorentz-matrix rule of Chapter 2.
key_equations.symbols: primed indices label new coordinates; Lambda Jacobian matrix

key_equations.name: Partial derivatives of x and y with respect to polar coordinates
key_equations.latex: \left(\frac{\partial x}{\partial r}\right)_\theta = \cos\theta,\ \left(\frac{\partial y}{\partial r}\right)_\theta = \sin\theta,\ \left(\frac{\partial x}{\partial\theta}\right)_r = -r\sin\theta,\ \left(\frac{\partial y}{\partial\theta}\right)_r = r\cos\theta
key_equations.meaning: Entries of the Jacobian from polar to Cartesian; they later build the basis vectors.
key_equations.symbols: subscript on the bracket is the variable held fixed

key_equations.name: Partial derivatives of r and theta with respect to Cartesian coordinates
key_equations.latex: \left(\frac{\partial r}{\partial x}\right)_y = \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}},\ \left(\frac{\partial r}{\partial y}\right)_x = \frac{y}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}},\ \left(\frac{\partial\theta}{\partial x}\right)_y = -\frac{y}{x^2+y^2},\ \left(\frac{\partial\theta}{\partial y}\right)_x = \frac{x}{x^2+y^2}
key_equations.meaning: Entries of the inverse Jacobian, from Cartesian to polar.

key_equations.name: Displacement components in polar coordinates
key_equations.meaning: The component law applied to an infinitesimal displacement; the matrix depends on position.

key_equations.name: Basis-vector transformation law
key_equations.meaning: Basis vectors transform with the inverse Jacobian, keeping X = X^mu e_mu invariant.

key_equations.name: Polar coordinate basis vectors
key_equations.meaning: Coordinate basis of plane polar coordinates in terms of the Cartesian basis; e_theta carries a factor r.

key_equations.name: Basis transformation in matrix form
key_equations.latex: \begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{e}_r & \mathbf{e}_\theta\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{e}_x & \mathbf{e}_y\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}(\partial x/\partial r)_\theta & (\partial x/\partial\theta)_r\\ (\partial y/\partial r)_\theta & (\partial y/\partial\theta)_r\end{pmatrix}
key_equations.meaning: Same result as 3.8, with basis vectors as a row multiplied on the right by the Jacobian.

key_equations.name: Normalized polar basis vectors
key_equations.meaning: The unit vectors of elementary treatments; they form a non-coordinate basis.

key_equations.name: Norms of the coordinate basis vectors
key_equations.meaning: e_theta grows with distance from the origin; these are the metric components g_rr and g_theta_theta of the plane in polar coordinates.

key_equations.name: Polar line element (implied by 3.11, not printed in the chapter)
key_equations.meaning: The flat metric of the plane in polar coordinates; equivalent to eqn 3.11 and explains the margin remark that s^2 is not r^2 + theta^2.

key_equations.name: Lie bracket of the coordinate basis
key_equations.meaning: Coordinate basis vectors commute, so a four-step loop along them closes.
key_equations.symbols: products of vectors are meaningful only as successive derivative operators

key_equations.name: Derivative of a function along a path
key_equations.meaning: Chain rule along a parametrized path.
key_equations.symbols: f scalar function; x^mu(lambda) path; lambda in [0, 1]

key_equations.name: Tangent operator along a path
key_equations.meaning: Has the form components times basis vectors, motivating the identification of e_mu with partial derivatives.

key_equations.name: Polar coordinate basis as partial derivatives
key_equations.meaning: Coordinate basis vectors are the partial derivatives with respect to the coordinates, which commute.

key_equations.name: Normalized polar basis as operators
key_equations.meaning: The unit theta vector is a position-dependent multiple of a partial derivative, which is what spoils commutation.

key_equations.name: Lie bracket of the normalized polar basis
key_equations.meaning: Non-zero, so the normalized basis is anholonomic; the sign says the loop gap points in the minus theta direction.

key_equations.name: General vector transformation rule
key_equations.meaning: The test any vector must pass under a general coordinate change.

key_equations.name: Coordinates related by coefficient matrix
key_equations.meaning: If A depends on position, partial x^{mu'}/partial x^nu is not A and x^mu fails 3.17; only constant A (linear homogeneous maps) lets coordinates act as vector components.
key_equations.symbols: A coefficient matrix, possibly position dependent

key_equations.name: Minkowski line element
key_equations.meaning: A non-Euclidean but flat metric with signature (-,+,+,+).
key_equations.symbols: eta Minkowski metric; units with c = 1

key_equations.name: Circumference of a circle on a sphere
key_equations.meaning: Circles on a sphere are shorter than 2 pi r; the Euclidean value returns when r is much smaller than R.
key_equations.symbols: r radius measured along the surface; R sphere radius

key_equations.name: Girard's theorem
key_equations.meaning: Angle sum of a spherical triangle exceeds pi by its area in units of R^2.
key_equations.symbols: alpha_i interior angles; A triangle area; R sphere radius. The running text prints the sum as over alpha_1, a typo for alpha_i.

key_equations.name: Cartesian x basis vector in the polar coordinate basis
key_equations.meaning: Inverse of the Example 3.2 transformation (Exercise 3.1).

key_equations.name: Cartesian y basis vector in the polar coordinate basis
key_equations.meaning: Inverse of the Example 3.2 transformation (Exercise 3.1).

key_equations.name: Derivatives of polar basis vectors
key_equations.meaning: Basis vectors change across the plane; the coefficients are the flat-space Christoffel symbols in polar coordinates (Exercise 3.2).

key_equations.name: Circle law in terms of curvature
key_equations.meaning: Rewrites 3.20 so that only the intrinsic quantity K appears.

key_equations.name: Curvature from small circles
key_equations.meaning: Operational, intrinsic definition of curvature: compare measured circumferences with 2 pi r for ever smaller circles. Follows from sinc x = 1 - x^2/6 + ...

key_equations.name: Area bookkeeping in the proof of Girard's theorem (unit sphere)
key_equations.meaning: The sphere minus two antipodal triangles is tiled by six strips, each a lune of angle alpha_i minus the triangle; the book gives the pieces, the assembled line is ours.

key_equations.name: Transformation to a uniformly rotating frame
key_equations.latex: t = t',\quad x = x'\cos\Omega t' - y'\sin\Omega t',\quad y = x'\sin\Omega t' + y'\cos\Omega t',\quad z = z'
key_equations.meaning: Coordinate change for Exercise 3.5.

key_equations.name: Minkowski metric in the rotating frame (our derivation, answer to Exercise 3.5)
key_equations.meaning: Still flat spacetime, but the metric is non-diagonal and position dependent: g_tt changes sign beyond the light cylinder rho = 1/Omega and the cross terms encode Coriolis effects and the Sagnac effect. Not printed in the chapter; derived by us and consistent with the answer in Appendix E (eqn E.15).

figures.label: Fig. 3.1(a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: A point with coordinates (x0, y0) in the Euclidean plane.
figures.visual_description: A square grid of fine grey lines with bold x (horizontal, arrow to the right) and y (vertical, arrow upward) axes crossing at the centre. A black dot sits in the upper-right quadrant; dashed lines drop from it perpendicularly to the axes, meeting them at tick labels x0 and y0.
figures.what_it_teaches: Cartesian coordinates label a point by projections onto perpendicular axes on a uniform grid.

redesign.idea: Twin-view coordinate explorer: one draggable point shown simultaneously on a Cartesian grid and a polar grid (combined with Fig. 3.1(b)).
redesign.interaction: Learner drags the point; readouts update (x, y) and (r, theta) live, with dashed projection lines on the Cartesian panel and the radius and angle arc on the polar panel; a toggle overlays both grids on one plane.

figures.caption_paraphrase: The same point described in polar coordinates by a distance r and an angle theta.
figures.visual_description: A disk-shaped polar grid of concentric grey circles and radial grey spokes. A bold line runs from the centre to a black dot up and to the right, labelled r; a dashed horizontal reference line leaves the centre to the right and a small arc labelled theta marks the angle between it and the radius.
figures.what_it_teaches: Polar coordinates label the same point by distance from the origin and angle; coordinate lines are circles and rays, not a uniform square grid.

redesign.idea: Merge with Fig. 3.1(a) into a single point-dragging demo, and add a small-step readout showing that a step d theta covers distance r d theta.
redesign.interaction: Learner nudges the point by fixed dr or d theta increments; a ruler shows the physical length of each step, which for d theta grows with r.

figures.label: Fig. 3.2(a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: The polar coordinate basis vectors e_r and e_theta do not keep a fixed size; e_theta lengthens with distance from the origin.
figures.visual_description: A polar grid with pairs of perpendicular arrows attached at several points. Every pair has one arrow pointing radially outward, all of about the same short length. The perpendicular (tangential, anticlockwise) arrow is tiny at a point close to the centre, moderate at mid radius (labelled e_r and e_theta at two points), and very long at points near and beyond the rim; one tangential arrow at the lower left extends well outside the disk.
figures.what_it_teaches: The coordinate basis vector e_theta has length r, so its size depends on where you are, while e_r stays unit length.
concepts: metric components as basis-vector dot products

redesign.idea: Basis-field painter: show e_r and e_theta as arrow fields over the plane with a toggle between coordinate and normalized versions (merging Figs. 3.2(a) and 3.2(b)).
redesign.interaction: Learner drags a probe point and sees both arrows with numerical lengths; a switch flips between coordinate basis (e_theta length r) and unit basis; a slider scales the displayed step in theta to show that one unit of theta is r units of distance.

figures.label: Fig. 3.2(b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: The normalized (non-coordinate) basis vectors keep unit length everywhere.
figures.visual_description: The same polar grid and the same attachment points as panel (a), with arrow pairs labelled e_r-hat and e_theta-hat. Now both arrows in every pair are the same short length whatever the distance from the centre; they still point radially outward and tangentially.
figures.what_it_teaches: Normalizing the polar basis keeps directions but removes the r-dependence of the size, at a cost revealed in Fig. 3.3.

redesign.idea: Second state of the basis-field painter described for Fig. 3.2(a).
redesign.interaction: Same controls as Fig. 3.2(a); the side panel displays the dot products e_r . e_r and e_theta . e_theta for the chosen basis.

figures.label: Fig. 3.3(a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: With the coordinate basis a loop ABCDE closes (A = E); e_theta must grow with r so that the outer arc BC is longer than the inner arc DA.
figures.visual_description: A quarter-disk polar grid with the origin at the lower left. A black dot marked A=E sits at modest radius near the bottom. An arrow runs radially outward from A to B; a long anticlockwise arc arrow runs from B to C at the larger radius; a straight arrow runs radially inward from C to D; a shorter clockwise arc arrow at the smaller radius runs from D back to the starting dot. Both arcs subtend the same angle. (The inventory mislabels this image as Fig. 3.2.)
figures.what_it_teaches: Stepping the same coordinate amounts forward and back returns you to the start: coordinate basis vectors commute.
concepts: loop-closure test for a coordinate basis

redesign.idea: Loop walker: a turtle takes steps of size epsilon along chosen basis fields (coordinate or normalized polar) in the order +A, +B, -A, -B and leaves a trail; the closure gap is measured.
redesign.interaction: Learner chooses the basis, the starting radius and the step size epsilon; the app shows the loop, reports the gap vector, and plots gap against epsilon on log axes so the epsilon^2 scaling and the predicted gap epsilon^2 [A, B] (here -epsilon^2 e_hat_theta / r) are visible.

figures.label: Fig. 3.3(b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: With normalized basis vectors the loop that starts at A ends at a different point E.
figures.visual_description: The same quarter-disk grid. From A an arrow goes radially outward to B; an anticlockwise arc of fixed length goes from B to C at the larger radius, sweeping a small angle; an arrow goes radially inward from C to D; a clockwise arc of the same length at the smaller radius sweeps a larger angle, overshooting A and ending at a black dot E just below (clockwise of) A.
figures.what_it_teaches: Equal-length steps in the theta-hat direction subtend different angles at different radii, so the loop fails to close: the normalized basis is anholonomic, with the gap in the minus theta direction as the bracket predicts.
concepts: loop-closure test for a coordinate basis

redesign.idea: Second mode of the loop walker (see Fig. 3.3(a)), with the gap vector highlighted and compared with the Lie-bracket prediction.
redesign.interaction: Learner flips to the normalized basis and watches E separate from A; dragging the loop outward shrinks the gap in proportion to 1/r.

figures.label: Fig. 3.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: A circle of radius r drawn on the surface of a sphere of radius R, placed humorously in a galaxy far away.
figures.visual_description: A hand-drawn sphere styled as the Death Star: an equatorial trench line and many small vertical hatch marks suggesting surface structures. In the upper right of the sphere a small circle is drawn on the surface with an arrow labelled r from its centre to its edge; a tiny twin-winged spacecraft floats to the right of the sphere.
figures.what_it_teaches: Circles can live on curved surfaces, with radius measured along the surface, and their circumference then differs from 2 pi r.
concepts: circumference of a circle on a sphere

redesign.idea: Circle-on-a-sphere lab: a 3D sphere with a geodesic circle whose surface radius r is set by a slider, alongside a live plot of C against r comparing 2 pi r with 2 pi R sin(r/R).
redesign.interaction: Learner drags r from zero past the equator (r = pi R / 2) to the antipode; the circle grows then shrinks; readouts show C, 2 pi r, the ratio, and the curvature estimate 3(2 pi r - C)/(pi r^3) converging to 1/R^2 as r shrinks. A second slider changes R.

figures.label: Fig. 3.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: Three great circles form a spherical triangle whose angles add to more than pi.
figures.visual_description: A sphere with shading hatch marks near its rim, crossed by three great circles: one roughly horizontal (like an equator) and two tilted ones that meet near the top. Front halves are solid lines, back halves dashed. Near the top the circles enclose a small triangle whose corner angles are labelled alpha_2 at the upper vertex, alpha_3 at the left and alpha_1 at the right.
figures.what_it_teaches: Triangles on a sphere are bounded by great circles and their angle sum exceeds pi.

redesign.idea: Spherical triangle builder: three draggable vertices on a 3D sphere joined by great-circle arcs, with live angle sum, area and excess.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags vertices; readouts show each angle, the sum, the area A/R^2 and the check sum - pi = A/R^2; a preset snaps to the octant triangle with three right angles.

figures.label: Fig. 3.6
figures.caption_paraphrase: The construction used to prove Girard's theorem.
figures.visual_description: A sphere drawn with the three great circles of Fig. 3.5 and the small triangle at the top labelled with alpha_1, alpha_2, alpha_3. Two strip-shaped regions bounded by great-circle arcs are shaded: one with dense diagonal hatching, visible at the upper left and along the right side, and one with stippled dots, visible at the lower left and lower right. Dashed lines mark arcs on the far side of the sphere.
figures.what_it_teaches: The sphere outside the triangle and its antipodal copy can be tiled by strips, each a lune of angle alpha_i with the triangle removed, which turns the angle sum into an area count.

redesign.idea: Animated proof: the sphere is cut into the triangle, its antipode and six strips; each lune lights up in turn with its area 2 alpha_i, and the running area total is shown until the identity emerges.
redesign.interaction: Learner steps through the proof with next/back buttons and can drag a vertex to see all areas and the final identity update together.

worked_examples.label: Example 3.1
worked_examples.problem: Transform the components of an infinitesimal displacement from Cartesian (dx, dy) to plane polar (dr, dtheta) using the component transformation law.
worked_examples.method: Compute the four partial derivatives of x and y with respect to r and theta and the four of r and theta with respect to x and y; arrange the latter as the Jacobian matrix acting on (dx, dy) and rewrite its entries using r and theta.
worked_examples.key_insight: The transformation matrix of Chapter 2 generalizes to a Jacobian whose entries depend on the point, which is the new feature of non-linear coordinate changes.
worked_examples.result: dr = cos(theta) dx + sin(theta) dy; dtheta = -(sin(theta)/r) dx + (cos(theta)/r) dy.
concepts: Jacobian matrix of a coordinate transformation

worked_examples.label: Example 3.2
worked_examples.problem: Find the polar coordinate basis vectors e_r and e_theta in terms of e_x and e_y.
worked_examples.method: Insert the derivatives of x and y with respect to r and theta into the basis-vector law e_{mu'} = (partial x^nu / partial x^{mu'}) e_nu; also write the result as the Cartesian basis row times the Jacobian matrix.
worked_examples.key_insight: Mechanically applying the law yields a basis in which e_theta carries a factor r, unlike the familiar unit vectors, setting up the coordinate versus non-coordinate distinction.
worked_examples.result: e_r = cos(theta) e_x + sin(theta) e_y; e_theta = -r sin(theta) e_x + r cos(theta) e_y.

worked_examples.problem: Check whether the basis found in Example 3.2 is normalized and compare with the textbook unit vectors (worked in the prose after Example 3.2).
worked_examples.method: Take dot products using the Euclidean metric in the Cartesian basis; compare with e_hat_r and e_hat_theta; interpret via the four-step loop picture of Fig. 3.3.
worked_examples.key_insight: The r-dependent length of e_theta is exactly what makes the outer arc of a coordinate loop longer than the inner arc so that the loop closes.
worked_examples.result: e_r . e_r = 1 and e_theta . e_theta = r^2; the normalized pair is e_hat_theta = e_theta / r.
concepts: loop-closure test for a coordinate basis
metric components as basis-vector dot products

worked_examples.label: Example 3.3
worked_examples.problem: Show that basis vectors can be represented by partial derivatives and use this to test whether the coordinate and normalized polar bases commute.
worked_examples.method: Differentiate a scalar function along a parametrized path by the chain rule, strip off the function to obtain an operator with the form components times basis, identify e_mu with partial_mu, then apply the commutator of e_hat_r = partial_r and e_hat_theta = (1/r) partial_theta to an arbitrary function.
worked_examples.key_insight: Once vectors are derivative operators, the Lie bracket is a routine calculation: partial derivatives commute, but a position-dependent prefactor produces an extra term from the product rule.
worked_examples.result: [e_r, e_theta] = 0; [e_hat_r, e_hat_theta] = -(1/r^2) partial_theta = -e_hat_theta / r, which is non-zero.

worked_examples.problem: Decide whether the coordinates themselves transform like vector components (argument of Section 3.2 and footnote 4).
worked_examples.method: Write the coordinate relation with a coefficient matrix and compare the coefficients with the Jacobian; note that they agree only when the coefficients are constant. Footnote 4 points to Example 3.1: the displacement Jacobian does not turn (x, y) into (r, theta).
worked_examples.key_insight: The Jacobian is a local, point-by-point object that maps infinitesimal differences; applying it to finite coordinate values is meaningless unless the map is linear and homogeneous.
worked_examples.result: Position vector excluded from the list of genuine vectors; coordinates kept as labels. (Our check: the matrix of eqn 3.6 applied to (x, y) gives (r, 0), not (r, theta).)

worked_examples.label: Example 3.4
worked_examples.problem: Show by example that Euclid's circle and triangle results fail on the surface of a sphere of radius R.
worked_examples.method: Quote the circumference of a circle of surface radius r and Girard's angle-sum formula, then examine the limits of small r and small area; proofs are left to Exercises 3.3 and 3.4.
worked_examples.key_insight: Deviations from Euclidean results are controlled by size relative to the curvature radius, so a small enough patch always looks Euclidean.
worked_examples.result: C = 2 pi r sinc(r/R), tending to 2 pi r for r much less than R; angle sum = pi + A/R^2, tending to pi for A much less than R^2.
concepts: circumference of a circle on a sphere

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Puck's promise to put a girdle round the Earth: coordinates as a net thrown over a world so that positions can be named.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Frames the chapter's reluctant return from coordinate-free geometry to explicit coordinate grids needed for concrete problems.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Purely literary; says nothing about how coordinates transform or why some grids are better than others.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Newton's law viewed from a merry-go-round: the same motion acquires centrifugal and Coriolis terms.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Shows that complexity in component equations can be a property of the chosen frame, motivating geometric statements.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Rotating frames involve time-dependent coordinate changes; the chapter's later examples are static spatial coordinate changes, so the link is qualitative until Exercise 3.5.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Split-screen: a puck sliding freely on a rotating table seen from above in the inertial frame (straight line) and in the co-rotating frame (curving path with drawn Coriolis and centrifugal arrows).

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Walking a square: step out, step round, step back, step round again, and see whether you are home.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Gives a tangible criterion for holonomic bases: the loop closes only if the sideways steps scale with radius.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: With finite unit steps the picture is only qualitative; the precise statement concerns vanishing Lie brackets, with the gap scaling as step size squared. It must not be confused with the holonomy of parallel transport, which detects curvature.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: The loop-walker demo described for Fig. 3.3.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The chain rule looks like a vector: components dx^mu/dlambda times basis objects partial/partial x^mu.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: A formal resemblance is promoted to a definition, making basis vectors into operators whose commutators can be computed.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Presented as a trick; why a derivative operator deserves to be called a vector (linearity, Leibniz rule, tangent spaces) is deferred to Chapter 31.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: A curve on a colour-mapped scalar field: the learner slides along the curve and sees df/dlambda assembled as the tangent arrow's components times the gradient components.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: An arrow from New York to Tokyo would burrow through the Earth, while a route of tiny steps can stay on the surface.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Explains why finite displacement vectors are not objects of a curved space whereas infinitesimal ones are.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Relies on the Earth being embedded in 3D space; spacetime has no such embedding, so the arrow does not exist at all rather than going somewhere else.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Globe view with two pinned cities: toggle between the straight chord (dips inside, depth readout) and a great-circle path built from many short tangent arrows that each lie in the local tangent plane.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Growth of e_theta is not a bug but a feature.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Recasts the unsettling unnormalized basis vector as the property that ties basis vectors to coordinate steps.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Rhetorical rather than explanatory; the explanation comes from the loop picture and the operator identification.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A circle drawn on the Death Star: geometry on a big ball in space.
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: circumference of a circle on a sphere
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: A playful picture of a circle whose radius is measured along a spherical surface.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The drawn radius arrow does not make clear that r is measured along the surface rather than as a straight chord.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: The circle-on-a-sphere lab described for Fig. 3.4, with a toggle showing the surface radius versus the straight-line chord.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Curvature measured by a surveyor who compares circle circumferences with 2 pi r for smaller and smaller circles.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Exercise 3.3 turns the circumference deficit into a limit that defines curvature from inside the surface.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Works cleanly for 2D surfaces; in higher dimensions curvature has many components and needs the Riemann tensor.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Flatland surveyor game: the learner measures circles drawn with a string on hidden surfaces (plane, sphere, saddle) and must infer the sign and size of curvature from the data.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The coordinates of a point form the components of a vector (the position vector) in any coordinate system.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Coordinates transform by the full nonlinear coordinate map, not by the Jacobian, unless the map is linear and homogeneous; they are labels. Only infinitesimal displacements dx^mu transform as vector components.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In introductory mechanics and in special relativity with Lorentz transformations the position vector works perfectly.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Good basis vectors must always be of unit length, so an e_theta of length r is a mistake.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Coordinate basis vectors are sized to match unit steps in the coordinate; e_theta must have length r. Unit vectors are allowed but form a non-coordinate basis with different properties.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Elementary physics uses unit vectors r-hat and theta-hat exclusively.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Extra terms that appear when a law is written in rotating coordinates are new physical forces.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The centrifugal and Coriolis terms reflect the choice of frame; the underlying vector law is unchanged.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: People in rotating frames genuinely feel them and they are named 'forces'.

misconceptions_addressed.correction: In the book's usage a non-Euclidean metric can be flat: Minkowski spacetime has metric eta, not delta, yet no curvature.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Popular accounts of non-Euclidean geometry are all about curved surfaces, and the chapter's second example (the sphere) is curved.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Distance in polar coordinates obeys Pythagoras directly, ds^2 = dr^2 + dtheta^2.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The angular step has physical length r dtheta, so ds^2 = dr^2 + r^2 dtheta^2.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Treating any pair of coordinates as if they were Cartesian.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Any two points in a curved space are joined by a displacement vector belonging to that space.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: A finite straight arrow generally leaves the space (the chord from New York to Tokyo); vectors live at points and describe infinitesimal displacements or tangents.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In flat space a single arrow can join any two points and be slid around freely.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Without a position vector there can be no velocity vector.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Velocity is the tangent to the world line, built from infinitesimal displacements; it is reconstructed in Chapter 7.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Velocity was taught as the derivative of position.
concepts: four-velocity as tangent to a world line

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The Jacobian matrix can be applied to the coordinate values themselves to get the new coordinates.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The Jacobian maps differentials and vector components at a point; applied to (x, y) it gives (r, 0), not (r, theta).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: For Lorentz transformations the same matrix maps both coordinates and components.
concepts: Jacobian matrix of a coordinate transformation

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A non-zero Lie bracket between basis vectors means the space is curved.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The Euclidean plane is flat, yet the normalized polar basis has a non-zero bracket. Brackets diagnose whether a basis comes from coordinates; curvature is diagnosed by the Riemann tensor or by circle and triangle tests.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Both involve going round a loop and failing to return to the same state, and the chapter places the loop idea just before discussing non-Euclidean space.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The expression e_r e_theta - e_theta e_r multiplies two arrows together.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The bracket only makes sense with vectors acting as derivative operators on functions: apply one, then the other, and subtract.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The book writes the bracket as a product before introducing the operator interpretation.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A metric that looks complicated in some coordinates (position-dependent, with cross terms) must describe a curved spacetime.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Exercise 3.5 produces such a metric just by rotating the frame of flat Minkowski spacetime; flatness is a coordinate-independent property.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Curved-spacetime metrics like Schwarzschild's also have position-dependent components.

thought_experiments.name: Newton's law on a rotating platform
thought_experiments.setup: Describe the same freely moving particle in an inertial frame and in a frame rotating relative to it.
thought_experiments.lesson: The vector equation is identical, but its components in the rotating frame pick up pseudo-force terms, so statements free of coordinates are cleaner.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Rotating-table puck demo with a frame toggle and the component equations displayed for each frame.

thought_experiments.name: The four-step loop on a polar grid
thought_experiments.setup: Starting at a point, step along the first basis vector, then the second, then reverse the first, then reverse the second, once with coordinate polar basis vectors and once with unit ones.
thought_experiments.lesson: Coordinate basis steps close the loop; normalized steps leave a gap, which is the geometric content of a non-zero Lie bracket.
concepts: loop-closure test for a coordinate basis
thought_experiments.app_idea: Loop walker with step-size slider and gap-versus-step log plot.

thought_experiments.name: Arrow from New York to Tokyo
thought_experiments.setup: Imagine a two-dimensional world that is only the Earth's surface and try to draw the displacement vector between two distant cities.
thought_experiments.lesson: The straight arrow leaves the world; only chains of infinitesimal displacements lying in the surface are meaningful, so vectors must be local.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Globe with chord versus great-circle route, showing chord depth and local tangent planes along the route.

thought_experiments.name: Surveying circles on a sphere
thought_experiments.setup: An inhabitant of a sphere draws circles of known surface radius and measures their circumferences, shrinking the circles toward zero.
thought_experiments.lesson: The shortfall from 2 pi r, divided by r^3 and suitably scaled, reveals the curvature 1/R^2 without leaving the surface.
concepts: circumference of a circle on a sphere
thought_experiments.app_idea: Surveyor game on hidden surfaces with a data table and a curvature fit.

thought_experiments.name: Adding up triangle angles on a globe
thought_experiments.setup: Draw a triangle from three great-circle arcs on a sphere and add its interior angles; compare triangles of different sizes.
thought_experiments.lesson: The excess over pi grows with area, vanishing for small triangles; the octant triangle has three right angles.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Spherical triangle builder with live angle sum and area.

historical_notes.event: Axiomatic plane geometry in the Elements, including the triangle angle sum of 180 degrees.
historical_notes.significance: Defines the flat benchmark whose failure on curved surfaces the chapter uses to introduce non-Euclidean geometry.

historical_notes.event: Introduced the idea of locating points in the plane by a pair of numbers, the Cartesian coordinates.
historical_notes.significance: The standard coordinate system on Euclidean space and the starting point for all transformations in the chapter.

historical_notes.event: A footnote records that Harriot found the spherical-excess theorem later credited to Girard, drew the Moon through a telescope some months before Galileo, and found the law of refraction about twenty years before Snell, who was in turn preceded by Ibn Sahl centuries earlier.
historical_notes.significance: A reminder that naming conventions misattribute discoveries. (Our addition, not in the chapter: Girard published the theorem in 1629, and Harriot's lunar drawing dates from 1609.)

applications_and_observations.topic: How far a straight New York to Tokyo arrow would dip below the surface
applications_and_observations.details: Our estimate for the book's example: with Earth radius 6371 km and a great-circle distance of about 10,850 km, the central angle is about 1.70 rad (98 degrees). The chord is 2R sin(angle/2) and its deepest point lies R(1 - cos(angle/2)) below the surface.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Chord about 9,590 km versus surface route about 10,850 km; maximum depth about 2,170 km (our estimate).

applications_and_observations.topic: Circumference deficit of a large circle on the Earth
applications_and_observations.details: Our estimate using eqn 3.20: the fractional shortfall of C below 2 pi r is about r^2/(6R^2) for r much less than R. For a circle of surface radius 1000 km on the Earth it is roughly 0.4 percent; for a 1 km circle it is about 4 parts in 10^9.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: r = 1000 km: deficit about 0.41 percent (about 26 km of a 6,280 km circumference); r = 1 km: about 4e-9 (our estimates).

applications_and_observations.topic: Angle excess of the octant triangle
applications_and_observations.details: Our illustration of eqn 3.21: the triangle with vertices at the North Pole and two equator points 90 degrees apart covers one eighth of the sphere, so A/R^2 = pi/2 and its angle sum is 3 pi/2, three right angles.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Angle sum 270 degrees; excess 90 degrees = (4 pi R^2 / 8)/R^2 (our example).

applications_and_observations.topic: Light cylinder of the rotating-frame metric
applications_and_observations.details: Our extension of Exercise 3.5: in the rotating coordinates g_tt = -(1 - Omega^2 rho^2) with c = 1, which vanishes at rho = c/Omega, beyond which a point at rest in the rotating frame would have to move faster than light. For a frame rotating with the Earth this radius is far outside the Solar System's inner planets; for a millisecond pulsar it is only tens of kilometres.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Earth: Omega = 7.29e-5 rad/s gives c/Omega about 4.1e12 m (about 27 AU); pulsar with 1.6 ms period: c/Omega about 76 km (our estimates).

notation_and_conventions.convention: Minkowski line element written ds^2 = -dt^2 + dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2, signature (-,+,+,+), with c = 1.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Matches the rest of the book (see Appendix B).

notation_and_conventions.convention: delta_mu_nu for the Euclidean metric components (identity matrix), eta_mu_nu for the Minkowski metric.
A prime on the index, x^{mu'} or x^{alpha'}, marks components in the new coordinate system; the letter itself (mu or alpha) is not significant.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Example 3.1 uses alpha' for (r, theta) while the text uses mu'; footnote 4 swaps the roles to x^alpha = (x, y).

notation_and_conventions.convention: Lambda^{mu'}_nu = partial x^{mu'} / partial x^nu transforms components; Lambda^nu_{mu'} = partial x^nu / partial x^{mu'} transforms basis vectors. The two are inverse matrices.
notation_and_conventions.notes: The upper-left/lower-right ordering encodes which index is new; the book does not spell out the inverse relation here.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Bold letters for vectors, X = X^mu e_mu with upper-index components and lower-index basis vectors, summed by the Einstein convention.
e_hat_r, e_hat_theta denote unit-normalized basis vectors; unhatted e_r, e_theta denote coordinate basis vectors.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Chapter 10 uses hats for orthonormal frame components more generally.

notation_and_conventions.convention: (partial x / partial r)_theta indicates the variable held constant, in thermodynamics style.
e_mu is identified with partial/partial x^mu (often written partial_mu).
[X, Y] = XY - YX, understood as acting on functions.
sinc x = (sin x)/x (unnormalized, no factor of pi).
notation_and_conventions.notes: Some fields define sinc x = sin(pi x)/(pi x).

notation_and_conventions.convention: (3+1)-dimensional means three space coordinates and one time coordinate.

margin_notes.summary: Epigraph from A Midsummer Night's Dream, Puck's boast of circling the Earth in forty minutes, later reused as the image of a coordinate girdle.
Writes the Euclidean scalar product with the summation convention and shows delta_mu_nu as the 3 by 3 identity matrix.
Polar coordinates are the first case of curvilinear coordinates, where Pythagoras does not hold in its naive form (s^2 is not r^2 + theta^2).
Etymology of holonomy: Greek roots for 'whole' and 'law'.
Boxed pointer: the link between vectors and derivative operators is developed in Chapter 31, and non-coordinate bases return in Chapter 10.
Example 3.1 already shows the problem: the displacement transformation matrix does not convert the coordinate values (x, y) into (r, theta).
In the flat spacetime of special relativity the constant-coefficient condition holds, so the displacement vector causes no trouble there.
Slogan to remember: coordinates are not vectors.
The Fig. 3.4 caption jokes that the sphere is in a galaxy far, far away; the drawing is the Death Star.
Thomas Harriot wrote down Girard's theorem first, beat Galileo to a telescopic Moon drawing, and found the refraction law before Snell (though long after Ibn Sahl); credit is not always fair.

notable.summary: Express the Cartesian basis vectors e_x and e_y as combinations of the polar coordinate basis vectors, with coefficients written in x, y and r.

skills: expressing results in a curvilinear basis
notable.why_notable: The four coefficients obtained are the flat-space Christoffel symbols in polar coordinates, a direct preview of connection coefficients in Chapters 7 and 9.

notable.summary: Derive the circumference of a circle on a sphere by elementary geometry, rewrite it with K = 1/R^2, and show that K can be recovered as a limit of the circumference deficit for shrinking circles.
notable.why_notable: Gives the reader an operational, intrinsic definition of curvature well before the Riemann tensor.

notable.summary: Prove Girard's theorem on a unit sphere by noting that three great circles make two antipodal triangles and that the remaining area splits into strips of area 2 alpha_i minus the triangle area.
notable.why_notable: An elegant counting proof that links angle excess to area and hence to curvature; the scaffolding in the exercise is generous.

notable.summary: Push the coordinate change to a uniformly rotating frame through the Minkowski line element (which the exercise writes compactly as the self scalar product of the displacement dx) and find its form in the rotating coordinates.
notable.why_notable: Closes the loop with the chapter's opening about rotating frames and shows a flat spacetime whose metric is non-diagonal and position dependent yet time independent (the answer, also given in GA appE eqn E.15, is written out in key_equations).

exercises.solutions: GA appE gives answers to Exercises 3.2 (derivatives of the polar basis, eqns E.12-E.14, matching eqn 3.24), 3.3 (a one-line series expansion; the printed line is damaged in two ways: it expands sin(r/sqrt(K)) where sin(r sqrt(K)) is meant, and it shows a stray equals sign where 2 pi r should multiply (1 - K r^2/6 + ...); its smallness condition should read r much less than 1/sqrt(K)) and 3.5 (rotating-frame line element, eqn E.15, which agrees with the derivation in key_equations). No answers are given for 3.1 or 3.4.

difficulty.notes: Computationally light: partial derivatives, 2 by 2 matrices and trigonometry. Conceptually the chapter packs several deep ideas (coordinate versus non-coordinate bases, Lie brackets, vectors as derivatives, why coordinates are not vectors) into a few pages, treating some loosely and deferring justification to Chapters 10 and 31. The Section 3.2 argument blurs flat curvilinear coordinates with curved spacetime, and the term non-Euclidean is used more broadly than in mathematics, which can confuse careful readers. The sphere results are stated without proof, but the exercises supply scaffolded proofs.
